content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

input.summary:
I traced every claim limitation, every numbered part, and every structural, positional, flow-path, material and operational statement in draft/04 through draft/10, numerals.md, and all seven figure briefs back to the single USER passage (the disclosure, repeated verbatim as the first USER turn of the conversation). The only other conversation turn is labelled "YOU (the drafting agent)"; I treated its account of earlier FIG. 1 / FIG. 5 edits as context only, not as inventor support.

Clean parts of the ledger. Formalities match input/brief.md: title verbatim, no priority claim (02 "Not applicable."), no federally sponsored research (03 "Not applicable."), no means-plus-function language, three statutory classes (claims 1, 13, 17). The Background is generic prior-art characterisation citing no document, so nothing there needs inventor support. All 28 table numerals appear in the description, no description numeral is missing from the table, and each numeral carries one meaning across all seven briefs (e.g. 50 is the guide-duct channel in both FIG. 4 and FIG. 5; 54 is the same wall opening in FIG. 2 and FIG. 4). The section line is designated consistently as 7-7 in FIG-6.md (designation 7 repeated at both arrow ends), FIG-7.md, and draft/07. The FIG. 6 arrow direction (leftward) is geometrically consistent with FIG. 7 showing the shell's outer surface facing left and the stem projecting left in the exposed position. The three broken-line curves in FIG-1.md are designated FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 and match the three enlargement briefs and draft/07. FIG. 2's single mating channel on one long side wall is consistent with FIG. 1's single rib and with the FIG. 1 section plane cutting both cassettes. Claims 1-20 each trace to the disclosure, including the dependent limitations I checked closely: claim 12's pre-seating registration (supported by "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration"), claim 15's upward-opening channel (inherent in a "depending indexing rib" entering it from the lid above), claim 5's removable cassettes ("conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"), and claims 9-11 and 20 on the indicator. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains in any deliverable file, and no application text or Brief Description sentence broadens an embodiment ("by way of example", "any closed outline") to justify a renderer's visual choice.

Findings. Four items, three of them untraced technical substance that all sit in the figure briefs rather than in the application text:

1. Critical. FIG-1.md verbalises a flow topology the inventor never described: "Above the upper edges of the blocks the central space and both channels are continuous across the top of the body, so the stream entering at the centre divides into both channels." The disclosure gives only the sequence "enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts"; it never says where the stream crosses from the central space into the ducts, and never says the crossover is above the cassettes. This is a flow-boundary/topology assertion, which stays substantive even under a schematic convention. The Detailed Description (draft/08 para "The circulation path") correctly stays neutral, so deleting the brief sentence leaves the text consistent.

2. Critical. FIG-1.md fixes the peripheral outlet port's vertical end position against the retention ledge: the duct opens "through the body's outboard side below the projecting block", and FIG-4.md reinforces it with "The fragment is taken below the level of the inward projections of the wall bodies." The disclosure says only that the outlet openings are "aligned with"/"overlap the side supply passages" and that the feet press "against ledges of the shell"; it states no relation between port and ledge. Port end positions are expressly substantive even for schematic geometry.

3. Major. FIG-2.md adds a stepped frame profile at the retention joint: "The lower part of each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame." The disclosure discloses only "resilient feet of the spacer frame" pressed "against ledges of the shell". A step forming the bearing interface is contact topology at a functional joint, not a generic housing outline. The plainer "downwardly facing outboard surface" wording in FIG-1.md and FIG-3.md is inherent in feet bearing down on ledges and can stay.

4. Minor. draft/08 introduces "side walls 14" in the paragraph that says "Referring to FIG. 1", but FIG-1.md's numeral list omits 14 (it first appears in FIG. 3). The walls are already drawn in FIG. 1, so adding the numeral there is a one-line fix.

Every fix is a deletion or a minimal-substitution inside the figure brief that owns the statement; none requires adding a speculative shape, optional embodiment, or new structure to the application text. Note that I did not inspect rendered images, citations, or the prior_art/ files, and I express no view on patentability.

findings.fix: In figures/FIG-2.md, replace the two sentences "The lower part of each long side wall carries an outward step, shown schematically, having a downwardly facing surface outboard of the frame. Small blocks project down from that surface, two visible at the front, shown schematically." with "Small blocks, two visible at the front, shown schematically, project downward from a lower outboard portion of each long side wall." Keep the following sentence "These blocks are the resilient feet 58." and the numeral entry for 58 unchanged.
